links.note: 771 has a warrior warn enemies not to stand before his lord (என்ஐமுன் நில்லன்மின்), since many who did now stand as memorial stones (கல்நின்றவர்). 894 states the rule behind the warning: for the unable to do harm to the able is like beckoning Death with the hand (கூற்றத்தைக் கையால் விளித்தற்று). The battlefield taunt and the political maxim give the same counsel, one from the strong side and one addressed to the weak.

771 dismisses the enemy by pointing to the many (பலர்) who faced his lord and became stones. 763 asks what it matters if a host of rats roars like the sea, since they perish when the cobra merely breathes (நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்). Both say numbers on the other side count for nothing against one real fighter; Parimelazhagar reads 763 as the hero not fearing a crowd of non-heroes.

771 is a warrior's boast about a might that turns opponents into memorial stones. In 1088 a lover says his பீடு, which even enemies who had not met him feared in battle (ஞாட்பினுள் நண்ணாரும் உட்கும்), has broken before her bright forehead. The Book of Love borrows the same figure of the warrior whose name alone frightens foes, here as a speaker's way of measuring her effect on him.

772 says holding the spear that missed an elephant (யானை பிழைத்த வேல்) is sweeter than holding the arrow that hit a forest hare. 596 says to think only of rising, and that even if the aim is thrust aside it has the nature of not being thrust aside (தள்ளினும் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து). Both value the high aim over the outcome; 772 puts in a hunting image what 596 states as a rule for ambition.

772 prefers the failed throw at an elephant to the successful shot at a hare, and Manakkudavar takes it with 771 as saying the warrior should send the weak away and fight those who can oppose him. 861 advises the reverse: avoid meeting the strong (வலியார்க்கு மாறேற்றல் ஓம்புக) and keep up enmity against the weak (மெலியார்மேல் மேக பகை). The conflict holds if 772 is read as a rule for choosing opponents and 861 as Parimelazhagar reads it; it is the warrior's pride against the king's policy. Kalaignar's gloss of 861 turns it into fighting the strong, which would remove the conflict.

773 says fierceness is called great manhood (பேராண்மை), but that helping the foe when something befalls him (ஊராண்மை) is its edge, அதன் எஃகு. 759 says to make wealth because no steel (எஃகு) is sharper for cutting down enemies' pride. The same word for a blade names two different things that finish an enemy's hostility: generosity in one verse, wealth in the other.

773 makes help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; Parimelazhagar illustrates it with the king of Ayodhya telling his disarmed enemy to go and come back tomorrow. 987 asks what use worth (சால்பு) is if one does not do what is sweet even to those who did one harm (இன்னா செய்தார்க்கும் இனியவே). The ideal of the worthy person in the chapter on சால்பு appears here as the height of a soldier's manhood.

In 774 a warrior who has thrown his spear at an elephant pulls out the spear stuck in his own body and laughs (மெய்வேல் பறியா நகும்). 621 advises laughing when trouble comes (இடுக்கண் வருங்கால் நகுக), since nothing presses it back as well. The wounded warrior's laugh is a battlefield instance of the general counsel; in 774 the laugh is also joy at finding a weapon.

774 shows a man who keeps fighting with a spear in his body, having spent his own on an elephant (களிறு). 597 says the strong-minded do not give way in ruin, like the bull elephant that holds its ground when hit by a sheaf of arrows (புதையம்பிற் பட்டுப் பாடூன்றும் களிறு). The elephant that is the warrior's target in 774 is the model of the same steadiness under wounds in 597.

775 asks whether it is not a rout (ஒட்டு in this edition, which Parimelazhagar glosses as turning the back) for the fierce if the eye glaring at the enemy closes in a blink when a spear is thrown. 686 requires the envoy to be one who does not fear the eye (கண் அஞ்சான்), which Parimelazhagar explains as the hostile king's angry stare; 585 says the same of the spy. Holding one's gaze under threat is a test in the court as on the field.

775 treats a single blink (இமைப்பின்) before a flung spear as equal to flight. In 1129 the woman says she will not blink because her lover, who lives in her eyes, would be hidden (இமைப்பின் கரப்பாக்கு அறிவல்). Both make the refusal to blink a measure of devotion, to valour in one and, in the speaker's conceit, to the beloved in the other.

In 776 the warrior goes over his days and puts among the wasted (வழுக்கினுள் வைக்கும்) every day on which he took no noble wound (விழுப்புண்). 38 says that if one does good so that no day falls away unused (வீழ்நாள் படாஅமை), it becomes a stone blocking the road of further lives. The same daily reckoning is applied with different entries: wounds for the soldier, good deeds for the person seeking release.

777 says that for those who want fame that circles the earth and do not want life (வேண்டா உயிரார்), tying on the war-anklet is an adornment. 235 says a ruin that is growth and a death that is existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) are possible only for the skilled, which Parimelazhagar explains by the body of fame outliving the body of flesh. 235 gives the reasoning for the warrior's choice in 777.

777 describes warriors who prefer fame (இசை) to life. 1017 says those ruled by shame give up life for shame and will not give up shame for life (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர்). Both rank a value above staying alive; in one it is public renown won in battle, in the other an inner restraint.

778 says warriors who do not fear for their life when battle comes (உறின் உயிர் அஞ்சா) do not lose their ardour even if their lord is angry (இறைவன் செறினும்). 690 defines the envoy as one who secures his lord's good (இறைவற்கு உறுதி) without holding back even if it brings his own end (இறுதி பயப்பினும்). Soldier and envoy share disregard for their own life in service; the soldier's zeal, on Parimelazhagar's reading, even outruns the king's order to stop.

778 says the lord's anger does not reduce the standing or ardour (சீர்) of fearless warriors. 895 says those who have drawn the anger of a king of fierce might (வேந்து செறப்பட்டவர்) will not survive anywhere they go. Both use the verb செறு for the king's anger; 778 marks a case where it is harmless, anger at excess of loyal zeal, while 895 concerns those who offend the powerful, whom Parimelazhagar takes to be rival kings.

779 asks who could fault for failure (பிழைத்தது ஒறுக்கிற்பவர்) those who die so as not to break what they vowed (இழைத்தது இகவாமை); Parimelazhagar explains that dying before the vow is accomplished still counts as keeping it. 772 says the spear that missed (பிழைத்த வேல்) the elephant is better to hold than the arrow that hit a hare. Both verses turn on பிழை, a miss, and deny that it is a disgrace when the attempt was great.

664 says saying is easy for anyone and doing as one has said is hard (சொல்லிய வண்ணம் செயல்). 779 takes the hardest case, a sworn vow in battle, and says the one who dies in the attempt cannot be blamed for failing. Death in the effort is accepted as having kept one's word, a limit on how literally 664's standard is applied.

780 says a death that fills with tears the eyes of those who maintained one is worth getting even by begging (இரந்துகோள் தக்கது உடைத்து). 220 says that if ruin comes through ஒப்புரவு, that ruin is worth getting even by selling oneself (விற்றுக்கோள் தக்கது உடைத்து). The two verses share one formula, in which a loss is made desirable by paying for it in the most degrading way the book knows, and apply it to a soldier's death and a giver's ruin.

780 holds that death in battle mourned by one's lord is to be sought. 235 says a death that is really existence (உளதாகும் சாக்காடு) is hard to come by except for the skilled. Both treat a certain kind of death as an achievement and not a loss; 780 names the sign of it, the tears of the one who sustained the warrior (புரந்தார்கண் நீர்மல்க).

781 asks what is as hard to make as friendship (செயற்கரிய யாவுள நட்பின்). 443 says that to cherish the great and make them one's own (தமராக் கொளல்) is the rarest of rare things (அரியவற்றுள் எல்லாம் அரிது). The chapter on the king's advisers and the chapter on friendship both open from the difficulty of winning the right people.

781 says no guard is as hard for hostile action to get past as friendship (வினைக்கரிய யாவுள காப்பு). 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin and an inner fort enemies cannot destroy (உள்ளழிக்கலாகா அரண்). The book names two protections as unsurpassed, one inside the person and one in his ties to others.

781 praises friendship as the best protection. 815 says the poor friendship of small people, which gives no safety even after it is made (செய்து ஏமம் சாரா), is better not had than had. The protection claimed in 781 belongs only to friendship with the right people; made with the wrong ones it guards nothing.

782 says the friendship of the wise fills like the crescent (பிறை நிறை நீர) and that of fools shrinks like the moon after full. 425 says understanding is what neither opens nor closes (மலர்தலும் கூம்பலும் இல்லது), which Parimelazhagar takes as friendship with the great that stays level and does not first bloom and then shut. Both reject the friendship that swells and fades; 782 praises steady growth where 425, on that reading, praises constancy.

782 contrasts friendships that grow and friendships that wane according to the kind of person. 811 says that with people without character, however ardent they look, it is better for the friendship to shrink than to grow (பெருகலிற் குன்றல் இனிது). The waning that 782 observes in bad friendships is in 811 what one should want for them.

783 says the bond with people of character gives more the more it is practised (பயில்தொறும்), as a book gives more delight the more it is studied (நவில்தொறும் நூல்நயம்). In 1110 a lover says that each closer union with her (செறிதோறும்) is like learning, where each thing known shows what was not known before (அறிதோறு அறியாமை கண்டற்று). Both use study as the model of a relationship that deepens with repetition, friendship in one and, in the lover's words, desire in the other.

783 says that with people of character (பண்புடையாளர்) the bond grows sweeter with practice. 811 says that with those who lack character (பண்பிலார்), friendship is better shrinking than growing, even if they seem to drink one up with affection. The reward of long practice in 783 depends on பண்பு; without it, more closeness is worse.

784 says friendship is not for laughing together but for going ahead and rebuking (இடித்தல்) when the friend oversteps. 448 says a king without people who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத) will perish even with no one to destroy him. The same verb marks what a friend owes a friend and what a counsellor owes a king.

784 denies that laughter is the purpose of friendship (நகுதற் பொருட்டன்று). 817 says that what comes from enemies is worth ten crore times more than friendship that is only of the laughing kind (நகைவகையர் ஆகிய நட்பு). The chapter on bad friendship condemns the very thing 784 excludes from friendship's definition.

784 gives rebuke as friendship's purpose. 795 turns it into a test for choosing friends: examine and take the friendship of those able to speak so that one weeps, to rebuke (இடித்து) and to teach what is proper. What 784 says a friend is for, 795 tells the reader to look for beforehand.

785 says neither union nor long acquaintance is needed (புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா), since shared feeling alone gives the claim of friendship (நட்பாங் கிழமை). 801 defines old friendship (பழைமை) as friendship that in no way cuts down that same claim (கிழமை), the liberties of intimacy. One verse derives the claim from feeling without long familiarity and the other from long familiarity, so they give கிழமை two sources.

Manakkudavar reads 785 as saying many days of acquaintance are not needed to judge a friendship, because for those of the same understanding (உணர்ச்சி) one meeting gives the claim. 792 says the friendship of one who does not examine again and again (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான்) ends in grief that kills him. On Manakkudavar's reading the two differ on whether friendship can safely be formed quickly; on Parimelazhagar's, 785 only says that feeling, more than contact, is what makes the bond, and there is no conflict.

786 says friendship in which only the face smiles is not friendship (முகநக நட்பது நட்பன்று), and that friendship in which the heart within smiles is. 824 says to fear deceivers who smile sweetly with the face and are bitter within (முகத்தின் இனிய நகாஅ அகத்தின்னா). The face and heart contrast that defines true friendship in 786 becomes in 824 the mark of a false friend to be feared.

786 says friendship of the face alone is not friendship. 830 advises that when the time comes for an enemy to act as a friend, one should befriend with the face, leave off friendship in the heart (முகநட்டு அகநட்பு ஒரீஇ), and later drop even that. The face-only friendship 786 excludes is recommended in 830 as a deliberate policy toward enemies, which fits 786 because it is not meant as friendship.

786 locates friendship in the heart's smile and not the face's. 93 says virtue lies in looking kindly with a glad face (முகத்தான் அமர்ந்து) and then speaking sweet words that come from the heart (அகத்தானாம் இன்சொல்). Both pair முகம் and அகம்; in speech the book asks for both together, and in friendship it says the face without the heart counts for nothing.

787 says friendship removes one from ruinous ways, sets one on the path (ஆறுய்த்து) and shares the suffering in ruin. 422 says understanding does not let the mind go wherever it goes, but turns it from evil and steers it toward good (தீதொரீஇ நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது). The friend does for a person from outside what understanding does from within, described with the same verb உய்.

787 ends with the friend who suffers along in ruin (அழிவின்கண் அல்லல் உழப்பது). 799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin (கெடுங்காலைக் கைவிடுவார்) burns the heart even when remembered at the hour of death. 799 shows the cost of the failure of the third duty that 787 lists.

788 says friendship removes distress there and then (ஆங்கே), like the hand of one whose garment slips. 102 says help given at the right time (காலத்தினாற் செய்த நன்றி), though small, is far greater than the earth. 788's image explains what timeliness means in 102: help that arrives without being asked and without delay.

In 788 the hand goes at once to the slipping garment (உடுக்கை). In 1023, for one who says he will raise his family, தெய்வம் tucks up its garment (மடிதற்று) and goes ahead of him. Both use a gesture with one's clothing for help that comes unasked and promptly, from a friend in one and from the divine in the other.

789 places friendship's throne in supporting the friend without wavering wherever it is possible (ஒல்லும்வாய் ஊன்றும் நிலை). 818 says to let slip without a word the friendship of those who make difficult a task they could do (ஒல்லும் கருமம் உடற்றுபவர்). The same word for what lies within one's power sets the standard in 789 and identifies the friend who fails it in 818.

789 defines the height of friendship as a firm state of propping the other up (ஊன்றும் நிலை). 449 says those without the support of a prop (மதலையாம் சார்பு) have no standing (நிலை), as those without capital have no profit. 789 describes the supporter and 449 the one who needs supporting, in the chapter on a king's reliance on the great.

790 says friendship looks shabby (புல்லென்னும்) even when friends dress it up in words (புனையினும்) such as 'they are this to us and we are that to them'. 978 says greatness always bows while smallness adorns itself in self-admiration (அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து). In both, the verbal ornament is the sign of the lesser thing: real friendship, like real greatness, does not advertise itself.

790 distrusts the declaration of how close two friends are; Parimelazhagar says that speaking of 'they' and 'we' already introduces a separation. In 1209 a woman says her life is ending as she thinks of the unkindness of the man who used to say 'we are not separate' (வேறல்லம் என்பார்). Her complaint is a speaker's case of what 790 states in general: saying the closeness did not make it so.
